planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; this cross of Meiwa kumquat and Satsuma mandarin was released by a USDA breeder in 1932.

directions: Nippon orangequat produces small, sweet, deep-orange fruit with an edible peel, eaten whole like a kumquat but with a milder, more orange-like flavor than Nagami or Meiwa. The tree is notably thornless even when young, making it pleasant to work around and harvest, and it holds fruit attractively through winter. It shares the cold hardiness typical of kumquat-derived hybrids, tolerating brief dips into the high teens Fahrenheit once established. Grow it as a specimen or large container plant, feeding with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season and providing winter protection north of zone 8b.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; kabosu is grown almost exclusively as a souring agent rather than for fresh eating.

directions: Kabosu is a tangy, aromatic Japanese citrus grown chiefly in Oita Prefecture, closely related to but larger and more mellow than sudachi. Fruit is harvested green and unripe from late summer into autumn, when its juice is squeezed over grilled fish, sashimi, hot pot dishes, and noodles for a bright, minty-citrus tartness. The tree is moderately cold-hardy for citrus, and mature specimens can shrug off brief drops to around 20F, though young trees need frost protection. Grow it like other cool-adapted mandarin relatives, in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and regular feeding during the growing season.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

common_name: Australian Blood Lime (Red-Fleshed Finger Lime-Mandarin Hybrid)
scientific_name: Citrus australasica x Citrus reticulata 'Australian Blood Lime'

planting.note: Plant in spring in frost-free areas or a large container; this selection combines red finger lime with the Ellendale mandarin.

directions: This Australian hybrid crosses the red finger lime with an Ellendale mandarin to produce egg-shaped, burgundy-skinned fruit filled with tangy, ruby-red vesicles resembling citrus caviar. It bears a resemblance to finger lime in leaf and habit but flowers and fruits on a somewhat sturdier framework. Fruit ripens in winter and is prized by chefs for garnishing seafood and cocktails or for pressing into a striking pink-red juice. Give it full sun, well-drained soil, and frost protection, since it is hardy only to around 25-30F and best suited to warm, essentially frost-free gardens or a container that can be moved under cover.

planting.note: Grow outdoors only in frost-free zones; elsewhere keep as a container plant that overwinters indoors near a bright window.

directions: This sport of the standard calamondin displays leaves irregularly splashed with cream and white, and even the young green fruit shows attractive light striping before ripening to orange. It is grown chiefly as a compact ornamental houseplant or patio specimen, its variegated foliage and abundant small, tart fruit making it a favorite for containers. Care matches the plain calamondin: full sun, rich well-drained soil kept evenly moist, and regular citrus fertilizer through the growing season. Variegated growth is often somewhat slower and less vigorous than the green-leaved form, so avoid overpotting and protect it from hard frost.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

planting.note: Plant in spring; this seed accession collected along the Yangtze River is among the most cold-hardy true citrus and can be sited outdoors well beyond typical citrus range with winter protection.

directions: Yuzu Ichandrin is a naturally occurring hybrid of Ichang papeda and mandarin, grown for its intensely fragrant, lemon-lime-flavored, seedy 3-inch fruit used for zest, juice, and preserves rather than fresh eating. It is exceptionally cold-tolerant for citrus, with mature wood reported to survive brief exposure near 0F, making it one of the few citrus relatives worth trying in marginal zone 7b-8 gardens with a sheltered microclimate. The tree is notably thorny and vigorous, so allow generous space and prune to keep fruit within reach. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, mulch the root zone for winter, and expect fruit to ripen in late fall.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

planting.note: Plant in spring in a warm, sheltered spot or large container; this dense, thornless small tree is grown as much for ornament as for its bitter fruit.

directions: Chinotto is a compact, thornless, slow-growing citrus historically cultivated on the Italian and French Riviera, prized for its small, dense, myrtle-like foliage and long-held crop of small round bitter oranges. The fruit is the traditional flavoring source for chinotto soda and is also candied whole, much like miniature Seville oranges. Its tidy habit and fragrant white spring flowers make it an outstanding container or patio specimen even where fruit is not harvested. Grow in full sun with rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil, and protect from hard freezes, since it tolerates only brief dips into the low-to-mid 20s Fahrenheit.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

common_name: Australian Round Lime (Dooja, Native Round Lime)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun; this is the largest-growing of the Australian native citrus and needs more room than finger lime or desert lime.

directions: Known to Aboriginal Australians as dooja, this rainforest-margin native from subtropical Queensland is the largest of the wild Australian citrus, forming a substantial shrub or small tree with glossy dark-green leaves and pinkish-white spring flowers. Its knobbly-skinned, spherical fruit ripens greenish-yellow from early to mid-winter and carries a thick, edible, aromatic peel traditionally candied or ground into a spicy paste similar to kaffir lime zest. It tolerates light frost and drought once established but grows best with full sun, rich well-drained soil, and regular water through the warmer months. Because of its eventual size it makes a better large hedge, screen, or open-ground specimen than a container plant, though young trees can be kept compact for some years in a large pot.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
